subject: Career
title: The Art of the Professional Email
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Art of the Professional Email.

hook.text: The average professional receives 121 emails per day. Yours has three seconds to prove it's worth reading.

buildup.text: Subject lines determine if your email gets opened. Vague subjects like 'Quick question' get ignored.

discovery.text: The inverted pyramid: lead with the ask, then provide context, then add details if needed.

twist.text: Long emails don't show thoroughness — they show you couldn't prioritize your thoughts.

climax.text: Structure: specific subject → one-line ask → brief context → clear next step with deadline.

punchline.text: If your email needs a TL;DR, rewrite the email.

quiz.question: How should you structure a professional email?
options: Lead with the ask, then provide context and a clear next step
Keep the request in the last paragraph

details.summary: Effective professional emails follow a structure of clear subject line, concise opening, organized body, and explicit call to action. Most business emails are scanned in under ten seconds, so frontloading the key message and minimizing length dramatically increases the chance of a response.
details.whyItMatters: The average professional receives over 120 emails per day. Emails that are clear, scannable, and action-oriented get faster responses and reduce unnecessary reply chains.
takeaways: Lead with the ask or key information in the first sentence
Keep emails under five sentences whenever possible
Use bullet points for any list of more than two items

faq.question: What makes a good email subject line in a professional setting?
faq.answer: A strong subject line is specific and action oriented. Instead of 'Update,' write 'Q3 Budget Approval Needed by Friday.' Include the topic, the action required, and any deadline so the recipient can prioritize without opening the email.

faq.question: How do I write emails that busy executives will actually read?
faq.answer: Use the BLUF method: Bottom Line Up Front. State the decision needed or key insight in the first line. Follow with no more than three supporting bullets. End with a clear next step and deadline. Executives scan; make every word count.
